# Book I, Proposition 45

*A parallelogram equal to a given rectilineal figure*

[Euclid's proof](#euclids-proof) · [In Lean](#in-lean) · [What it rests on](#what-it-rests-on) · [Mishnah](#mishnah)

> To construct, in a given rectilineal angle, a parallelogram equal to a given rectilineal figure.

**In Lean:** ✅ proved for a restricted statement (a figure of two triangles) · Euclid's argument

## Euclid's proof

<p align="center"><img src="../../figures/I/45.svg" alt="Euclid's figure for Proposition I.45, with Heath's letters. H is drawn on D, as the Lean has it; Heath draws the parallelogram apart." width="360"></p>

<p align="center"><em>H is drawn on D, as the Lean has it; Heath draws the parallelogram apart.</em></p>

Let ABCD be the given rectilineal figure and E the given rectilineal angle; thus it is required to construct, in the given angle E, a parallelogram equal to the rectilineal figure ABCD.

Let DB be joined, and let the parallelogram FH be constructed equal to the triangle ABD, in the angle HKF which is equal to E; [I. 42] let the parallelogram GM equal to the triangle DBC be applied to the straight line GH, in the angle GHM which is equal to E. [I. 44]

Then, since the angle E is equal to each of the angles HKF, GHM, the angle HKF is also equal to the angle GHM. [C.N. 1]

Let the angle KHG be added to each; therefore the angles FKH, KHG are equal to the angles KHG, GHM.

But the angles FKH, KHG are equal to two right angles; [I. 29] therefore the angles KHG, GHM are also equal to two right angles.

Thus, with a straight line GH, and at the point H on it, two straight lines KH, HM not lying on the same side make the adjacent angles equal to two right angles; therefore KH is in a straight line with HM. [I. 14]

And, since the straight line HG falls upon the parallels KM, FG, the alternate angles MHG, HGF are equal to one another. [I. 29]

Let the angle HGL be added to each; therefore the angles MHG, HGL are equal to the angles HGF, HGL. [C.N. 2]

But the angles MHG, HGL are equal to two right angles; [I. 29] therefore the angles HGF, HGL are also equal to two right angles. [C.N. 1]

Therefore FG is in a straight line with GL. [I. 14]

And, since FK is equal and parallel to HG, [I. 34] and HG to ML also, KF is also equal and parallel to ML; [C.N. 1; I. 30] and the straight lines KM, FL join them (at their extremities); therefore KM, FL are also equal and parallel. [I. 33]

Therefore KFLM is a parallelogram.

And, since the triangle ABD is equal to the parallelogram FH, and DBC to GM, the whole rectilineal figure ABCD is equal to the whole parallelogram KFLM.

Therefore the parallelogram KFLM has been constructed equal to the given rectilineal figure ABCD, in the angle FKM which is equal to the given angle E.

Q. E. F.

From [`Elements/BookI/Prop45.lean`](../../Elements/BookI/Prop45.lean). Euclid's sentences are the `--` comments, and our own notes are in `/- … -/`; the lines under each sentence are the Lean that carries it out. The list below marks where a step needs a word of its own; the `/- … -/` notes in the listing explain smaller adjustments.

**How the Lean follows the text**

- **Carried.** "Let DB be joined, and let the parallelogram FH be constructed equal to the triangle ABD…" I.42 builds FH on half of BD itself, so H falls on D: the Lean writes D wherever Euclid writes H, and its parallelogram KFLM overlaps ABCD.

```lean
/-- To construct, in a given rectilineal angle, a parallelogram equal to a given rectilineal figure. -/
theorem Prop45 {A B C D E₁ E E₂ : Point} (hABD : Triangle A B D) (hDBC : Triangle D B C)
    (hE : Triangle E₁ E E₂) :
    ∃ K F L M : Point, Parallelogram K F L M ∧ ∠ F K M = ∠ E₁ E E₂ ∧
      quadArea K F L M = △ A B D + △ D B C := by
  -- Let ABCD be the given rectilineal figure and E the given rectilineal angle; thus it is
  -- required to construct, in the given angle E, a parallelogram equal to the rectilineal
  -- figure ABCD.
  -- Let DB be joined, and let the parallelogram FH be constructed equal to the triangle ABD,
  -- in the angle HKF which is equal to E; [I. 42] let the parallelogram GM equal to the
  -- triangle DBC be applied to the straight line GH, in the angle GHM which is equal to
  -- E. [I. 44]
  /- I.42 builds on half of the triangle's own base, so KH lies along BD and H
     falls on D: the Lean writes D wherever Euclid writes H, and in our figure KFLM
     overlaps ABCD. K lies between B and D, and F is on A's side of BD. -/
  obtain ⟨K, F, G, hBKD, hFA, hFKHG, hHKF, hFH⟩ := Prop42 hABD hE
  have hGHK : Triangle G D K := hFKHG.1.symm.swap_right.triangle.bac
  /- I.44's point for the side is taken across GH from K, so that KH and HM are
     "not lying on the same side", as I.14 will ask. -/
  obtain ⟨P, hPK, -⟩ := exists_oppositeSidesOf hGHK []
  obtain ⟨L, M, hMP, hGHML, hGHM, hGM⟩ := Prop44 hGHK.ne₁₂ hDBC hE hPK.triangle
  have hMK : OppositeSidesOf M K G D := hMP.trans_opposite hPK
  have hKD : K ≠ D := hGHK.ne₂₃.symm
  have hGD : G ≠ D := hGHK.ne₁₂
  have hFK : F ≠ K := hFKHG.1.1
  -- Then, since the angle E is equal to each of the angles HKF, GHM, the angle HKF is also
  -- equal to the angle GHM. [C.N. 1]
  have hHKF_GHM : ∠ D K F = ∠ G D M := CommonNotion1 hHKF hGHM
  -- Let the angle KHG be added to each; therefore the angles FKH, KHG are equal to the angles
  -- KHG, GHM.
  have hsum₁ : ∠ F K D + ∠ K D G = ∠ K D G + ∠ G D M := by
    rw [angle_symm hFK hKD.symm, hHKF_GHM, add_comm]
  -- But the angles FKH, KHG are equal to two right angles; [I. 29] therefore the angles KHG,
  -- GHM are also equal to two right angles.
  have hFG_KH : SameSideOf F G K D := hFKHG.rotate.sameSideOf.symm
  have h29a : ∠ F K D + ∠ K D G = ∟ + ∟ := Prop29.interior hFKHG.1.swap_left hFG_KH
  have hKHG_GHM : ∠ K D G + ∠ G D M = ∟ + ∟ := hsum₁.symm.trans h29a
  -- Thus, with a straight line GH, and at the point H on it, two straight lines KH, HM not
  -- lying on the same side make the adjacent angles equal to two right angles; therefore KH is
  -- in a straight line with HM. [I. 14]
  have hKHM : Between K D M := Prop14 hMK.symm (by
    rw [angle_symm hGD hKD]
    exact hKHG_GHM)
  -- And, since the straight line HG falls upon the parallels KM, FG, the alternate angles MHG,
  -- HGF are equal to one another. [I. 29]
  have hFK_HG : SameSideOf F K D G := hFKHG.rotate.rotate.sameSideOf
  have hMD : M ≠ D := ne_of_between (between_symm hKHM)
  obtain ⟨KM, hK_KM, hM_KM⟩ := Postulate1 K M (ne_of_between_ends hKHM)
  have hD_KM : OnLine D KM := on_line_of_between_ends hKHM hK_KM hM_KM
  obtain ⟨FG, hF_FG, hG_FG⟩ := Postulate1 F G hFKHG.2.2.1.symm
  have hKM_FG : Parallel KM FG := hFKHG.2.parallel hK_KM hD_KM hG_FG hF_FG
  have hMHGF : AreParallel M D G F :=
    AreParallel.of_parallel hMD hFKHG.2.2.1 hM_KM hD_KM hG_FG hF_FG hKM_FG
  have hMF : OppositeSidesOf M F D G := (hFK_HG.trans_opposite hMK.symm.swap).symm
  have hMHG_HGF : ∠ M D G = ∠ D G F := Prop29.alternate hMHGF hMF
  -- Let the angle HGL be added to each; therefore the angles MHG, HGL are equal to the angles
  -- HGF, HGL. [C.N. 2]
  have hsum₂ : ∠ M D G + ∠ D G L = ∠ D G F + ∠ D G L := CommonNotion2 hMHG_HGF rfl
  -- But the angles MHG, HGL are equal to two right angles; [I. 29] therefore the angles HGF,
  -- HGL are also equal to two right angles. [C.N. 1]
  have hML_HG : SameSideOf M L D G := hGHML.sameSideOf.swap
  have h29c : ∠ M D G + ∠ D G L = ∟ + ∟ := Prop29.interior hGHML.2.swap_right hML_HG
  have hHGF_HGL : ∠ D G F + ∠ D G L = ∟ + ∟ := CommonNotion1 hsum₂.symm h29c.symm
  -- Therefore FG is in a straight line with GL. [I. 14]
  have hFL : OppositeSidesOf F L D G :=
    hFK_HG.trans_opposite (hML_HG.symm.trans_opposite hMK.swap).symm
  have hFGL : Between F G L := Prop14 hFL hHGF_HGL
  -- And, since FK is equal and parallel to HG, [I. 34] and HG to ML also, KF is also equal and
  -- parallel to ML; [C.N. 1; I. 30] and the straight lines KM, FL join them (at their
  -- extremities); therefore KM, FL are also equal and parallel. [I. 33]
  obtain ⟨-, hFK_GH, -, -, -⟩ := Prop34 (A := F) (B := G) (C := K) (D := D) hFKHG
  obtain ⟨-, hGH_LM, -, -, -⟩ := Prop34 (A := G) (B := L) (C := D) (D := M) hGHML
  have hlen : ‖K F‖ = ‖M L‖ :=
    CommonNotion1 ((len_symm K F).trans hFK_GH) (hGH_LM.trans (len_symm L M)).symm
  obtain ⟨KF, hK_KF, hF_KF⟩ := Postulate1 K F hFK.symm
  obtain ⟨ML, hM_ML, hL_ML⟩ := Postulate1 M L hGHML.1.2.1
  obtain ⟨GD, hG_GD, hD_GD⟩ := Postulate1 G D hGD
  have hKF_GD : Parallel KF GD := hFKHG.1.swap_left.parallel hK_KF hF_KF hD_GD hG_GD
  have hML_GD : Parallel ML GD := hGHML.1.symm.parallel hM_ML hL_ML hG_GD hD_GD
  have hKF_ML : KF ≠ ML := fun e => by
    have hK_ML : OnLine K ML := e ▸ hK_KF
    have : ML = KM := line_unique (ne_of_between_ends hKHM) hK_ML hM_ML hK_KM hM_KM
    exact hML_GD.not_onLine (this ▸ hD_KM) hD_GD
  have hpar : AreParallel K F M L :=
    AreParallel.of_parallel hFK.symm hGHML.1.2.1 hK_KF hF_KF hM_ML hL_ML
      (Prop30.parallel hKF_GD hML_GD hKF_ML)
  have hdir : SameSideOf F L K M := by
    have hF : SameSide F G KM := hFG_KH.sameSide hK_KM hD_KM
    have hL : SameSide L G KM := hGHML.rotate.sameSideOf.sameSide hD_KM hM_KM
    exact SameSideOf.of_line (ne_of_between_ends hKHM) hK_KM hM_KM
      (same_side_trans (same_side_symm hF) (same_side_symm hL))
  obtain ⟨-, h33⟩ := Prop33 hpar hlen hdir
  -- Therefore KFLM is a parallelogram.
  have hKFLM : Parallelogram K F L M := ⟨hpar.swap_right, h33.symm.swap_right⟩
  -- And, since the triangle ABD is equal to the parallelogram FH, and DBC to GM, the whole
  -- rectilineal figure ABCD is equal to the whole parallelogram KFLM.
  have hwhole : quadArea K F L M = △ A B D + △ D B C := by
    rw [quadArea_add_of_parallelograms hFKHG.rotate.reverse hGHML.rotate.reverse hKHM hFGL,
      quadArea_reverse K D G F, hFKHG.quadArea_rotate, hFH,
      quadArea_reverse D M L G, hGHML.quadArea_rotate, hGM]
  -- Therefore the parallelogram KFLM has been constructed equal to the given rectilineal
  -- figure ABCD, in the angle FKM which is equal to the given angle E.
  refine ⟨K, F, L, M, hKFLM, ?_, hwhole⟩
  rw [angle_onRay_right (OnRay.of_beyond hKHM) hFK, angle_symm hFK hKD.symm]
  exact hHKF
  -- Q. E. F.
```

**Reading the figure**

- [`between_cases`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L74) (used here): Of three different points on a straight line, one is between the other two. (Between 6)
- [`between_of_between_left`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L66): If B is between A and C, and D is between A and B, then D is between A and C. (Between 4)
- [`between_of_between_right`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L70) (used here): If B is between A and C, and C is between B and D, then B is between A and D. (Between 5)
- [`between_symm`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L43) (used here): If B is between A and C, it is between C and A. (Between 1)
- [`centre_inside`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L35): The centre of a circle is inside it. (Generalities 3)
- [`circles_meet`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L201): If each circle passes through a point inside the other, the circles cut one another. This is the step Euclid takes for granted in I.1. (Intersection 5)
- [`circles_meet_of_on_inside_outside`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L195): Two circles cut one another if the first passes through a point A inside the second, and a point B outside the second is inside or on the first. (Intersection 4, in LeanEuclid's corrected form)
- [`circles_meet_same_side`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Constructions.lean#L81): Two circles that cut one another do so on each side of the straight line through their centres. (Intersections 8)
- [`exists_point`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Constructions.lean#L26) (used here): Let a point be taken. (Points 1)
- [`exists_point_between`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Constructions.lean#L38): Let a point be taken between B and C. (Points 3)
- [`exists_point_on_line`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Constructions.lean#L29) (used here): Let a point be taken on the straight line L. (Points 2)
- [`exists_point_on_line_off_line`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Constructions.lean#L34) (used here): Let a point be taken on L, not on the different straight line M. (Points 2, with "distinct from M")
- [`exists_point_opposite_side`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Constructions.lean#L46) (used here): Let a point be taken on the other side of L from B. (Points 6)
- [`inside_not_on`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L38): A point inside a circle is not on it. (Generalities 4)
- [`line_circle_between`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Constructions.lean#L69): A straight line through a point B inside a circle, heading out to a point C outside it, cuts the circle between B and C. (Intersections 4)
- [`line_circle_beyond`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Constructions.lean#L75): A straight line through a point B inside a circle, produced beyond B away from C, cuts the circle there. (Intersections 5)
- [`line_unique`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L28) (used here): Two points determine a straight line. (Generalities 1)
- [`lines_meet_of_opposite_sides`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L179) (used here): A straight line joining points on opposite sides of L crosses L. (Intersection 1)
- [`ne_of_between`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L46) (used here): A point between two others differs from the first. (Between 1)
- [`ne_of_between_ends`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L49) (used here): The ends of a finite straight line differ. (Between 1)
- [`not_between_of_between`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L52) (used here): If B is between A and C, then A is not between B and C. (Between 1)
- [`not_between_of_between_between`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L79): If B is between A and C, and also between A and D, then B is not between C and D: C and D lie on the same side of B. (Between 7)
- [`not_on_line_of_same_side`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L92) (used here): Points on one side of a straight line are not on it. (Same side 3)
- [`on_line_of_between`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L56) (used here): A straight line through A and B, with B between A and C, passes through C. (Between 2)
- [`on_line_of_between_ends`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L61) (used here): A straight line through A and C passes through every point between them. (Between 3)
- [`pasch1`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L106): If A and C are on the same side of L, so is any point between them: if B is between A and C, then A and B are on the same side of L. (Pasch 1)
- [`pasch2`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L111) (used here): If B is between A and C, A is on L and B is off it, then B and C are on the same side of L: a straight line that leaves L at A does not cross it again. (Pasch 2)
- [`pasch3`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L114) (used here): A straight line through a point between A and C separates them. (Pasch 3)
- [`pasch4`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L119) (used here): If two different straight lines L and M meet at B, and A and C are points of M, different from each other and from B, that are not on the same side of L, then B is between A and C. (Pasch 4)
- [`same_side_or`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L99) (used here): A straight line has only two sides. (Same side 5)
- [`same_side_refl`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L85) (used here): A point off a straight line is on the same side of it as itself. (Same side 1)
- [`same_side_symm`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L89) (used here): If A is on the same side of a straight line as B, then B is on the same side as A. (Same side 2)
- [`same_side_trans`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L96) (used here): Two points on the same side of a straight line as a third point are on the same side as each other. (Same side 4)
- [`triple_incidence1`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L131) (used here): Take B on L, C on M and D on N, three straight lines through A. If C lies within the angle BAD (on D's side of L and on B's side of N), then B and D are not on the same side of M: the straight line AC separates them. (Triple incidence 1)
- [`triple_incidence2`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Diagram.lean#L139): Take B on L, C on M and D on N, three straight lines through A, with B other than A and D off M. If C and D are on the same side of L, and B and D are not on the same side of M, then B and C are on the same side of N: C lies within the angle BAD. (Triple incidence 2)

**Lengths, angles and areas**

- [`angle_add_of_inside`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Transfer.lean#L54): If D lies within the angle BAC, then BAC is made up of BAD and DAC. (Diagram-angle 2)
- [`angle_eq_of_same_rays`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Transfer.lean#L72) (used here): The angle doesn't change if its arms are traced through other points on the same rays. (Diagram-angle 4)
- [`angle_symm`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Metric.lean#L26) (used here): The angle ABC is the angle CBA. (Metric 4)
- [`area_add_of_between`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Transfer.lean#L88) (used here): Cutting a triangle in two from a vertex adds up. (Diagram-area 2)
- [`area_congruent`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Metric.lean#L43): Triangles equal in all their sides and angles are equal in area. Euclid uses this without comment once he has shown two triangles congruent. (Metric 9)
- [`area_degenerate`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Metric.lean#L32) (used here): A "triangle" with a repeated corner has no area. (Metric 6)
- [`area_eq_zero_of_on_line`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Transfer.lean#L80) (used here): A "triangle" whose corners lie on one straight line has no area. (Diagram-area 1)
- [`area_rotate`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Metric.lean#L35) (used here): The triangle ABC is the triangle CAB. (Metric 8)
- [`area_swap`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Metric.lean#L38) (used here): The triangle ABC is the triangle ACB. (Metric 8)
- [`eq_of_len_eq_zero`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Metric.lean#L17): A finite straight line with distinct ends has length. (Metric 1)
- [`inside_of_len_lt`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Transfer.lean#L33): A point nearer the centre than the circumference is inside. (Diagram-segment 4)
- [`len_add_of_between`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Transfer.lean#L21): If B is between A and C, then AB and BC together make up AC. (Diagram-segment 1)
- [`len_lt_of_inside`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Transfer.lean#L37): A point inside is nearer the centre than the circumference. (Diagram-segment 4)
- [`len_self`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Metric.lean#L20): The "straight line" from a point to itself has no length. (Metric 1)
- [`len_symm`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Metric.lean#L23) (used here): The straight line AB is the straight line BA. (Metric 3)
- [`same_ray_of_angle_eq_zero`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Transfer.lean#L49): If the angle BAC is nothing, C lies on the ray from A through B. (Diagram-angle 1)

**Superposition**

- [`superposition`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Superposition.lean#L30): **Superposition.** The triangle ABC can be applied to the straight line L with A on D, B on the ray from D through G, and C on the side of L where H is, without changing any side or angle.

**Laws of magnitude**

- [`add_assoc`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L23) (used here): Adding three magnitudes in a row, it makes no difference whether the first two or the last two are added first. (System E §3.5)
- [`add_comm`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L26) (used here): The order of adding does not matter. (System E §3.5)
- [`add_lt_add_right`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L45): Adding the same thing to both sides keeps "less than". (System E §3.5)
- [`add_zero`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L29) (used here): Adding nothing changes nothing. (System E §3.5)
- [`lt_irrefl`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L32): No magnitude is less than itself. (System E §3.5)
- [`lt_trans`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L35): What is less than the less is less still. (System E §3.5)
- [`lt_trichotomy`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L39): Of two magnitudes, one is less, or they are equal, or the other is less. (System E §3.5)
- [`not_lt_zero`](../../Elements/Foundations/Tacit/Magnitudes.lean#L42): Nothing is less than zero. (System E §3.5)

</details>

## Mishnah

_Our commentary: what Euclid assumes, what Lean made us say out loud, and how the result looks by modern means._

**"Let DB be joined."** Euclid cuts the figure into two triangles: ABD goes to I.42, and DBC to I.44, which applies a parallelogram equal to it to GH, a side of the first. More sides mean more triangles, each applied in turn to the side the last one left. So we give the figure as Euclid cuts it, the sum of ABD and DBC, for our `quadArea` would read ABCD along the other diameter, AC, which falls outside the figure when it has a corner pointing inwards at B or D.

**Dividing with a straight line.** Heath takes stock: "We have now learnt how to represent any rectilineal area, which can of course be resolved into triangles, by a single parallelogram having one side equal to any given straight line and one angle equal to any given rectilineal angle" (vol. 1, p. 347). A rectangle stands for a product, so applying one to a given straight line is, in his words, "the geometrical equivalent of algebraical *division*" (p. 347). The last step, a square equal to the figure, waits for II.14.

**"The squaring of the circle as well."** Proclus guesses that "it was in consequence of this problem that the ancient geometers were led to investigate the squaring of the circle as well" (Heath, vol. 1, p. 347): if any straight-sided figure can be made a parallelogram, why not a circle? Archimedes, he adds, proved a circle equal to the right-angled triangle whose sides about the right angle are the circle's radius and perimeter. But no construction with straight lines and circles can lay that perimeter out straight, as Ferdinand von Lindemann showed in 1882.

**The modern way.** The figure's area is ½|(B − A) × (D − A)| + ½|(B − D) × (C − D)|, where u × v is the determinant of u and v. The parallelograms share the side a = KF = GH and the angle E, so their breadths KH and HM, each a triangle's area divided by a sin E, add up to KM.

## Further reading

- For the figure that no ruler and compass can turn into a square, the circle, Felix Klein's [*Famous Problems of Elementary Geometry*](https://archive.org/details/famousproblemsof00kleiiala) (1897, free online), which shows why.
- For whether applying an area really is division, as the modern way says, Jens Høyrup's ["What is 'geometric algebra', and what has it been in historiography?"](https://doi.org/10.3934/Math.2017.1.128) (2017, free online), a guided tour of fifty years of argument, and a gentle way into it.
